issues.legal_issue: Joint family property does not lose its character merely because one coparcener remains, while a widow of a deceased coparcener continues to have a right of maintenance from it.
material_facts: The property was ancestral joint family property held by two brothers.
After one brother died, the surviving brother was the sole coparcener.
The deceased brother’s widow remained alive and had a right to maintenance from the property.
issues.conclusion: The property retained its character as joint family property in the hands of the sole surviving coparcener.
issues.legal_principle: A joint family may consist of a single male member and widows of deceased male members; a temporary reduction of the coparcenary to one person does not convert joint family property into that person’s separate property. The rights of family members, including a widow’s right to maintenance, remain relevant. The Court followed Gowli Buddanna v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Mysore and applied Attorney General of Ceylon v. A.R. Arunachalam Chettiar.

rule.if: joint_family_property_character_dispute and (only_one_coparcener_remains and widow_of_deceased_coparcener_is_alive and widow_has_maintenance_right)

predicates.joint_family_property_character_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property retains its joint family character when only one coparcener remains.
predicates.only_one_coparcener_remains: One member of the family remains as the sole coparcener holding the property.
predicates.widow_of_deceased_coparcener_is_alive: The widow of a deceased coparcener remains alive.
predicates.widow_has_maintenance_right: The widow has a right to maintenance from the family property.
predicates.property_retains_joint_family_character: The property continues to be joint family property despite being held by a sole coparcener.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the character of joint family property, and one coparcener remains while a deceased coparcener’s widow is alive with maintenance rights from the property, the property retains its joint family character.

issues.legal_issue: A child adopted by a widow becomes the adopted son of her deceased husband and a coparcener in the husband’s joint family property.
material_facts: The property retained its joint family character after one brother became the sole surviving coparcener.
The surviving brother’s sister-in-law, who was the widow of the deceased coparcener, adopted a child.
The adoption was made under the law governing adoptions after its commencement.
The adopted child was the deceased coparcener’s nephew through the widow’s marriage.
issues.conclusion: The adopted child became the son of the widow and her deceased husband, and a coparcener with the surviving brother in the joint family property.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 11 and 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, adoption severs the child’s ties with the birth family and replaces them with ties in the adoptive family. Read with section 14, this means that a child adopted by a widow is absorbed into the family to which she belonged and is treated as the son of her deceased husband; section 14(4), which treats a later husband as the child’s stepfather, supports that implication. The Court approved Arukushi Narayan v. Janabai Sama Sawat.

predicates.adoption_based_coparcenary_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an adopted child gains a coparcenary interest through the adoptive family.
predicates.valid_adoption_by_widow: A widow validly adopts a child.
predicates.adoptive_widow_was_member_of_deceased_hu: The adopting widow belonged to the family of her deceased husband.
predicates.joint_family_property_retains_its_charac: The property remains joint family property when the adoption takes effect.
predicates.adopted_child_is_son_of_deceased_husband: The adopted child is treated as the deceased husband’s son and becomes a coparcener in the family property.

issues.definition: In an adoption-based coparcenary dispute, when a widow validly adopts into the family of her deceased husband and the property remains joint family property, the adopted child becomes the deceased husband’s son and a coparcener.

issues.legal_issue: The rights of an ordinary tenant in agricultural land are heritable under the tenant’s personal law unless a special statutory provision provides otherwise.
material_facts: The deceased held rights as an ordinary tenant in agricultural land.
The claimant, as the deceased’s adopted son and successor under personal law, claimed those tenancy rights.
The relevant statute contained provisions on mutation applicable to all classes of tenants but no special rule excluding inheritance of ordinary tenancy rights.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary tenancy rights were heritable under personal law, and the adopted son was entitled to succeed to them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 86 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 applies to all classes of tenants and contemplates succession or transfer of tenancy rights. Sections 87 and 89 address ordinary tenants and sub-tenants but do not make ordinary tenancy rights non-heritable. In the absence of a special statutory provision, heritability is governed by the tenant’s personal law.

rule.if: claim_to_inherit_ordinary_tenancy and deceased_held_ordinary_tenancy_rights and no_special_rule_excludes_inheritance and claimant_succeeds_under_personal_law

predicates.claim_to_inherit_ordinary_tenancy: The proceeding concerns a claim to inherit an ordinary tenancy in agricultural land.
predicates.deceased_held_ordinary_tenancy_rights: The deceased held the agricultural land as an ordinary tenant.
predicates.no_special_rule_excludes_inheritance: No special statutory rule excludes inheritance of the ordinary tenancy rights.
predicates.claimant_succeeds_under_personal_law: The claimant succeeds to the deceased tenant’s rights under the applicable personal law.
predicates.ordinary_tenancy_rights_are_heritable_un: The ordinary tenancy rights pass by inheritance according to the tenant’s personal law.

issues.definition: When a claim concerns inherited ordinary tenancy rights, the deceased held those rights, no special rule excludes inheritance, and the claimant succeeds under personal law, the rights are heritable under personal law.

issues.legal_issue: A jurisdictional objection decided against a party below and not challenged in the High Court cannot be raised for the first time in a further appeal to the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court decided the jurisdictional objection against the respondent.
The respondent did not challenge those decisions on that issue in the High Court.
The respondent sought to raise the objection in the Supreme Court appeal.
issues.conclusion: The respondent could not raise the jurisdictional objection at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the procedural rule that a party may not raise in a further appeal an issue decided against it below when that decision was not challenged in the intermediate appeal.

predicates.further_appeal_to_supreme_court: The proceeding is a further appeal to the Supreme Court.
predicates.objection_decided_against_party_below: The jurisdictional objection was decided against the party by the lower courts.
predicates.objection_not_challenged_in_intermediate: The party did not challenge that decision in the intermediate appeal.
predicates.objection_cannot_be_raised_at_further_ap: The party is not permitted to raise the objection for the first time at the further appeal stage.

issues.definition: In a further appeal to the Supreme Court, an objection decided against a party below and not challenged in the intermediate appeal cannot be raised at the further appeal stage.
